content: Hi everyone! I have taken an interest in helping with the thermodynamic module of physlean.
Together with @Mitchell Scheffer we just issued our very first PR, about formalizing adiabatic transformations in the ideal gas
Our (tentative) next step will be to fomalize the ideal gas. We'll probably build a structure for it, but we'd love to know if the community has better ideas!

Hi, it's great to see this !
FYI you may be interested in this work in progress attempt to formalize Lieb-Yngvason. Of course it is a completely different approach, and I think PhysLean should have both, but it may help to see how to derive the axioms/assumptions you will have to make in your ideal gas structure.

Thank you for sending this, I didn't know about it. Yes, we should have both. Morally, what Lieb-Yngvason did was proving a bunch of things that are needed for a thermodynamic entropy to exist. While obviously I'll be assuming a bunch of properties of the entropy, as per Callen's axioms. It'd be great to find the proper way to connect these two approaches, although I'm not entirely sure how.

Hi all, I've opened a PR that links to the discussion happening in this thread:
https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/pull/1365

@Matteo Cipollina I spent some time working through the repo you linked here, and
you've covered substantial ground. I've used a lot of your ideas in my PR but haven't yet
added you as an author — please let me know and I'll be happy to make that change.

I'd also really appreciate your comments on the PR. The goal was to add something to Physlib
that would let us develop Callen-style macroscopic thermodynamics, hopefully port over your
work to finish the formalization of Lieb–Yngvason in Physlib, and, longer term, formally
connect the different interpretations of entropy. The PR aims to give a first look at that
connection goal as well.

Thanks!

Thank you so much for your reply @Matteo Cipollina

I have alot of comments on the PR already and was planning on splitting it up to bring more focus to the callen parts and LY parts seperately. However, please do give your comments on the PR when you get time and I will absorb them into the subsequent PR for just the LY part.

Would be great if we can reach the end goal of getting LY into physlib, especially since you have already done so much work :)

I'm resuming working on this, thanks to @Omar Aguilar who's been doing the heavy lifting to come up with a good design for the thermodynamics library. We think we have a good starting point and we'll send a few PR shortly

Amazing to hear @Fabio Anzà @Omar Aguilar and am very excited to see your PRs.

Just to point out I had also tried to do some work in Physlib#1365 on this topic on trying to create a foundation for callen style thermodynamics (though I have been unable to find the time to finish this :()

The files basic.lean, intensive.leanand extensive.leanin ./FundamentalRelation/ might be of interest to you with your design.

Though I would be very happy to hear that you guys have an even better design than what I have suggested!

I teach thermo with Callen and I’m trying to follow the “primitives” that Callen establishes: The postulates; Walls/Constraints; Closure relations; Intensive and Extensive. Just yesterday @Omar Aguilar was making the point that building a math library where to put a bunch of reusable results makes the code looks a lot more like Callen-style thermo. We’re not entirely there yet but it looks like a decent bet
A math library seperate from physlib?
If it helps we can use this thread to discuss and soundboard, I am also interested in thermodynamics in physlib (though your expertise definitely eclipses mine :sweat_smile: )
I mean a bunch of thermo-specific math results. Something like wrappers around specific results of math lib
Mhm true, though this can and should be placed within physlib

Yes, it should be 100% within physlib. The only question would be: should it be within thermo or within a physics-adapted-math-results folder. I discussed this with @Joseph Tooby-Smith some time ago but I don't think we reached an agreement
I think to start can be within the thermo folder, then as we iterate it will become quite obvious when things would need to go into the Physlib/Mathematics folder
I mean to say it should not block you opening a PR :)

Fabio Anzà said:

I mean a bunch of thermo-specific math results. Something like wrappers around specific results of math lib

If you have an example maybe we can discuss

Worth saying that we have refactored the ./Mathematics folder in physlib recently so this would be a good place for physics-adapted-math-results. But yeah, also no harm in getting this wrong initially - can always refactor or move later.

I was thinking something like the following:

  • Use ./Mathematics as much as possible
  • When things in there are not enough, first it goes into a thermo-math subfolder
  • Then, refactoring into ./Mathematics for broader use
    Makes sense?
To clarify on the refactor, Joseph refactored Mathematics into 2 main parts, stuff for mathlib under Mathematics/ForMathlib and then the rest of the the folder for physics associated math results
Also would be difficult to comment on the arrangement without seeing the lean code :/

I think this make sense, though am not 100% up to speed with what the results are you are talking about. If they are:

  1. General maths results which are used throughout physics, and have physics-specific flavour to them, them ./Mathematics seems correct.
  2. But if they are e.g. a specific framework for thermo, then I think in ./Thermodynamics in a specifically named subdirectory etc.

Makes sense. @Omar Aguilar is making sure that the code is a bit more polished before doing the PR. The idea is that these results are not general but specific to thermodynamics. They will be something like the technical appendices in Callen

Nice to meet you, @Nathaneal Sajan! Thanks for sharing your work, the fundamental relation files are very helpful.

The distinction @Joseph Tooby-Smith outlined makes sense to me too. And agreed, it’ll be easier to discuss the organization with the code in front of us. I’m currently polishing it for the first PR.
Hi Omar, nice to meet you too, am excited to see your PR :)

Hi, I can also share a bit of work we did on the thermodynamics of heterogeneous equilibria (liquid-gas equilibrium and the like). I cleaned up the repository a bit compared to the version we're activly working on.
Very interesting, thank you. This also has the math + physics design, but it's substance/model-based

Indeed, our main interest is to compare how the calculations in various models work for certain aspects, in particular for multicomponent mixtures. To do that comparison, we tried to push the common elements in the calculations as much as possible into the maths layer. It seems that this approach is very much complementary to what you have in mind, which appears to be to start from the mathematical foundations. Please feel free to re-use or modify whatever you can use from our work.

Hi @Omar Aguilar, have looked through your PRs. Firstly, they look great, super easy to review and the documentation is easy to read.

How I'm thinking about formalizing thermodynamics (the following might also be general to most formalizations) is that we need API for stating thermodynamic problems and then the convex analytic tools to study them. Physlib#1831 and Physlib#1833 provide useful vocabulary for the first part and look nicely scoped.

With Physlib#1834 we're begining to connect those two parts, so I'd be interested in how you plan on proceeding from here, just to get the full picture how the API works. For example, how would the postulates connect to the entropy derivatives needed to derive equal temperatures for two systems in thermal contact?

I can speak to some of this since we've been doing weekly back and forth with @Omar Aguilar to refine the design of the library. At the higher level, I think we're on the same page. First the proper language to state thermodynamic problems; Then tools to study them.

On the first part, my approach has been to find a way to have a "general thermodynamic substance" API that essentially represents Callen's axioms. One can then derive general consequences, like the equality of temperature in thermal equilibrium, without having to specify explicitly a fundamental relation, say S(U,V,N). Or, one can specify a specific fundamental relation and (A) prove or disprove that said relation satisfies Callen's axioms; or (B) go into proving specific properties of said substance.

About the tools, the main issue for me was to find ways to express in lean the "manipulating differentials" tools that thermodynamics relies on. I've made a couple of attempts in the past, using but I was not satisfied with anything. However, it looks like that was my limited capacity to write good Lean code since @Omar Aguilar has been able to use fderiv to get there.

We already have a bunch of other files but since we've been writing and re-writing every week, I've asked @Omar Aguilar to send the PRs a few at the time, once we feel the design is decent and there are no obvious expressivity holes.

Specifically to your question: the idea is to implement a single general tool that implements the following general statement. Given some thermal equilibrium system with walls that avoid transfer of extensive variables, if we change the state of some of these walls (e.g. the energy wall) then the general result is that the partial derivatives with respect to the variables that are allowed to flow have to be equal in the final equilibrium state
Currently, we can do it via the postulates or via another set of files that we have not yet shared. We'll be trying to consolidate that into a single route before submitting

I'm wondering here if we should try and connect things with the dimensions and units API from the off-set. I'm not sure how much work that would be, but would likely make the physics clearer, and also enable us to see where dimensions and units API falls down.
Did you have something specific in mind? A bunch of declarations about the units and dimensionalities of the core quantities defined? Entropy, energy, volume, work, heat etc?

We could, for example define: 

structure Volume where
   val : Real

On this put the instance CarrriesDimension. Then in EquilibriumState we could have Dimensionful Volume. This would mean that in EquilibriumState you have to give both a number and the units it is written in. Instead of defining Volume above, one could also use WithDim _.

Thank you for clarifying @Fabio Anzà. Would you be happy sharing some more code context? Perhaps share a test branch or maybe or even a few Lean theorem statements you’re working towards, this would help us review your design choices.

Alternatively, you could point your PRs at PhyslibAlpha and get them merged much quicker. That could let the work progress there while giving us more context for reviewing it for Physlib.

Thanks, @Joseph Tooby-Smith and @Nathaneal Sajan, for reviewing the PRs and for the helpful suggestions! I’ll work through the comments on the PRs today.

@Nathaneal Sajan , here’s our current thermal-equilibrium example on a test branch, with its dependencies included. It follows the derivation step by step through equations (2.30)–(2.37) in §2.4, “Thermal Equilibrium—Temperature,” of Callen’s second edition.

Thanks also for sharing your fundamental-relation work. The example uses your FundamentalRelation, ExtensiveState, temperature definition, and hasDerivAt_dS_dU lemma. These provide the connection between entropy variations and inverse temperatures in the equilibrium calculation. I’ll keep the reused and adapted code clearly attributed to you as the development evolves.

The example combines our wall constraints with an entropy-maximum hypothesis corresponding to Postulate II and entropy additivity from Postulate III. It derives equality of inverse temperatures, assuming an admissible nonzero first-order energy exchange.

With Fabio, I’m also developing a new implementation of the fundamental relation, building on your work. We want to separate the Postulate III properties and additional assumptions from the relation itself, so each theorem can use the hypotheses it needs. We also want to support both energy and entropy representations on equal footing.

Another design goal is to express the fundamental-relation differential as an equality between continuous linear maps, alongside the evaluated form in your fderiv_S_apply. This would make it easier to compose and rearrange differential identities while keeping their application to particular variations available.

The new formulation is still under development, and I’d welcome your thoughts on how these choices could fit with your development!

@Joseph Tooby-Smith , I’ll update the domain examples, coordinate representation, and file organization as I address the PR comments today.

I like the idea of connecting this with Physlib’s dimensions and units API from the get go! I’ll try incorporating it into the thermodynamics definitions and check how it carries through the differential calculations.

Apologies for my extremely delayed response to this, thank you for this message and your clarification - it was very helpful. I have broken up my response into 2 parts so that it's easier to follow :)

Separating the assumptions and exposing the differential as an equality of continuous linear maps both sound like useful directions. These are the points that help make the API useful, ideally we would want to be able to make these foundations such that downstream users never worry about any of the calculus and can freely use different assumptions.

One thing to note as you have used some of my code, this was still in an experimental phase (as you might have noticed). One important conclusion from some later investigations was to keep admissible domains system-dependent and avoid requiring positive internal energy universally, for example, an energy-reference change U'=U+cN can give admissible negative energies.

The other important point was to keep the domain and inverse/derivative relationships explicit. Those conversion requirements are separate from the convexity assumptions needed for stronger equilibrium results and later potentials.

This thermal example seems like a useful test to retain through the redesign and units integration as it helps ground certain decisions. As you can see, your design is evolving quite rapidly when having to account for the differential relationships, I am looking forward to see your redesign.

One general point, I think one would need some more references than just callen for formalizing thermodynamics. For example, when we have to think about the legendre transform, it's quite difficult to figure out exactly how one would formalize this by just using Callen. Some helpful references I came across were

Compositional thermodynamics - Baez et al
Fundamental Functions in Equilibrium Thermodynamics - Teg Horst

I am still going through the above but I think these might really help us pin down the mathematical structure that might work for us, they are quite heavy on the convex analysis, but we would not need to use the most advanced mathematical technology they suggest (eg. the category theory parts in Baez). But instead have an approximate version of some structures but design in such a way that later down the line one could "upgrade" to the most rigorous structures. Continuing the Legendre transform example, to be fully rigorous, one would need to consider the Legendre-Fenchel Conjugate, but (to the best of my knowledge) this is not available in mathlib, so it would be great to design something that allows us to get a version of this transform for the immediate physics goal, but still leave room for development when this becomes available in mathlib.

Thanks, @Nathaneal Sajan , for taking the time to write such a detailed response! Your point about system-dependent admissible domains is very helpful as I work on the redesign. I’ll follow that and avoid requiring positive internal energy universally (positivity restrictions also gave me some trouble with differentiation in Lean). And yes, I agree about keeping the derivative relationships and the conversion between energy and entropy representations explicit. The thermal-equilibrium example is helping me decide how much structure the fundamental relation needs.

Thanks also for sharing these references! I’ve mainly been following Callen so far to get things off the ground, and because its pedagogical style makes the derivations easier to follow and review. I’ll start looking into the sources you suggested and others as well. I agree that we should leave room for the more general and rigorous structures you describe as things develop.
